latency: In this book, a latency measurement records the time the website takes to handle a request.
observation: Each request contributes one measured response time to the sample.
observation window: The twenty requests were recorded during the same short stretch of time.
rank: In the sample, the rank gives a response time’s position from fastest to slowest.
median: middle value of an ordered sample
With twenty requests, the median is the midpoint between the 10th and 11th response times.
round up: move to the next whole number if needed
The nearest-rank method uses a whole-number position, even when the calculation gives a fraction.
nearest-rank method: a percentile rule based on sorted positions
Multiply the sample size by the desired fraction and round up to find the position in the sorted list.
percentile: value at or below which a specified share of observations falls
The 95th percentile describes a cutoff near the slow end of the measurements.
tail: part of a distribution containing extreme values
Here the tail refers to the relatively few requests that take much longer than most.
threshold: chosen cutoff for deciding what to count
The report can count requests that took more than one second.
sample size: number of observations in the sample
Here twenty requests means that each request accounts for five percent of the observations.
traffic mix: proportions of different kinds of requests
Tuesday has more ticket-buying requests relative to browsing requests than Monday.
break down: Separate figures for browsing and buying help explain why the overall number increased.
apparent: The overall number suggests the site became slower, while each activity takes the same time as before.
breakdown: A separate number for each tour might reveal which ticket purchases are affected by a delay.
